title: Scheme for Transport-based Global Entanglement Distribution using Quantum Processors
authors: Erik Lundblad, Mira Abu Yahia, Antonius Johannes Renders, Andreas Walther, Adam Kinos, Lars Rippe
abstract: We propose a scheme for distributing entanglement over global distances in a heralded manner by using satellites to physically transport entangled processor nodes with rare-earth-ion qubits. A full analysis of channel losses, errors and background light is performed to determine the fidelity and number of entangled pairs that can be distributed between two ground stations. We show that the scheme works already with a single satellite and can distribute close to the theoretical maximum number of entangled pairs that can be generated in a satellite overpass. In addition, we argue that in theory transportation-based schemes outperform other satellite-based schemes and can be scaled up to a constellation without additional channel losses. Daytime operation seems feasible as long as the sky is clear, with an EPR pair fidelity ranging from 99.3% at shorter network lengths to 93.9% with global coverage and can be further improved by active error correction or entanglement purification.
summary: The paper proposes a novel, highly efficient method for distributing entanglement globally using satellites equipped with rare-earth ion qubits. It models the entire process—from atmospheric channel loss to multi-stage entanglement swapping—to demonstrate that this transportation-based repeater scheme is superior to existing proposals. This work advances the feasibility roadmap for global quantum internet infrastructure.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a viable scheme for distributing quantum entanglement over global distances using satellite links.
main_result: A transportation-based, quantum repeater approach utilizing rare-earth ion qubits in satellites is theoretically shown to outperform other methods by minimizing link losses and achieving high fidelity (e.g., 93.9% globally).
method: The analysis combines theoretical modeling of free-space optical channel losses with quantum information protocols like heralded entanglement generation and deterministic entanglement swapping.
model_or_system: The system involves ground stations connected via Very Low Earth Orbit (VLEO) satellites carrying nodes based on rare-earth-ion qubits. The process models the sequential steps of generating, storing, and swapping entangled pairs across multiple passes.
key_observables: EPR pair fidelity ($F$), entanglement generation probability ($p_{HEG}$), achievable rate ($	ext{N}_{	ext{tot}}$), and background light induced error ($\epsilon_B$).
important_parameters: VLEO altitude (250 km), coherence time ($T_2 > 13$ hours), sky brightness ($H_b$), and various loss coefficients ($\eta_{at}, \eta_{SMF}$).
main_assumptions: The scheme assumes the feasibility of active error correction, sufficient qubit coherence times, and that background light noise can be quantified using Poisson statistics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the entanglement distribution process (Satellite $	o$ Ground $	o$ Swapping), performance comparisons between different protocols (e.g., transport vs. memory-based), and the dependence of fidelity on network length or error sources.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical link efficiency ($\eta_c$) via atmospheric modeling, to developing the quantum protocol using Markov chains for pair generation, and finally comparing this repeater scheme against direct relaying or memory-limited approaches.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenges of scaling quantum networks by providing a detailed theoretical framework for overcoming distance limitations inherent in photonic quantum communication.
